title: Design In-Memory File System
statement:
Design an in-memory file system. There is a single root folder `/`. Every folder can contain zero or more folders and text files. You can list the contents of any folder.

Paths are absolute: they start with `/` and components are separated by `/`. A component is a non-empty string of lowercase letters and digits. The path `/` is the root.

Support these operations:

- `mkdir path`: create the folder `path`, together with any missing folders on the way (like `mkdir -p`). Nothing happens if it already exists.
- `write path text`: append `text` to the file at `path`. If the file does not exist it is created first, and any missing parent folders are created too.
- `ls path`: if `path` is a folder, print the names of everything directly inside it, sorted in ascending lexicographic order, separated by single spaces, with a `/` appended to the name of each sub-folder (files have no suffix). Print `-` if the folder is empty. If `path` is a file, print just the file's name.
- `read path`: print the full content of the file at `path` (everything written to it so far, in order).

You may assume that no path is ever used both as a folder and as a file, that every path given to `ls` or `read` exists, and that `read` is only used on files. `text` is a single token without spaces.

For every `ls` and `read` operation print one line with its result.
inputFormat:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
Each of the next `n` lines is one operation: `mkdir path`, `write path text`, `ls path` or `read path`.
outputFormat: For each `ls` and `read` operation, in order, print one line with its result. The input contains at least one of them.
constraints: Each path has at most 20 components and at most 100 characters
The total number of names printed by all `ls` operations is at most 10^6

examples.input:
8
mkdir /docs/work
write /docs/notes hello
write /docs/notes world
ls /docs
read /docs/notes
ls /
ls /docs/notes
ls /docs/work
examples.explanation: `/docs/work` is created as a folder, and `/docs/notes` becomes a file whose content is `hello` followed by `world`. Listing `/docs` shows the file `notes` and the folder `work/`. Listing the root shows `docs/`. Listing a file prints its own name, and the empty folder `/docs/work` prints `-`.

examples.input:
5
write /a/b/c x
ls /a
ls /a/b
mkdir /a/z
ls /a
examples.explanation: Writing `/a/b/c` creates folders `a` and `b` and the file `c`. `/a` holds only `b/`; `/a/b` holds only the file `c`. After `mkdir /a/z`, `/a` holds `b/` and `z/`.

complexity.time: O(L) per operation, plus O(k log k) for sorting k names in ls
complexity.space: O(total size of all paths and file contents)

hints: Model the file system as a tree: a folder is a map from child name to child. Resolving a path is just walking down one component at a time.
Store folders as dictionaries and files as their content, so that `ls` can tell the two kinds apart and print the `/` suffix.
Do not keep a flat list of full paths and scan it for each `ls`; that makes every listing cost the size of the whole file system.

from typing import List


def run(ops: List[List[str]]) -> List[str]:

def main():
    lines = sys.stdin.read().split('\n')
    first = lines[0].split()
    n = int(first[0])
    ops = [lines[1 + i].split() for i in range(n)]
